# Bosonic Character of Cooper Pairs in Fermi Gases with Tunable Interactions

## Overview and Motivation

The study of paired atoms in ultracold Fermi gases offers a unique window into the crossover between fermionic and bosonic quantum statistics. This investigation examines the two-particle wave function of paired atoms across a range of interaction strengths, exploiting the experimental control afforded by Feshbach resonances. By tuning an external magnetic field near a Feshbach resonance, one can continuously adjust the s-wave scattering length $a$, thereby traversing the BEC-BCS crossover—from a regime of tightly bound bosonic molecules to one of weakly correlated Cooper pairs reminiscent of conventional BCS superconductivity. This tunability provides an ideal theoretical and experimental platform for probing how the quantum statistical nature of paired fermions evolves as the character of the pairing interaction changes.

## Quantifying Bosonic Character

Central to this analysis is the development of a quantitative measure for the bosonic character of the Cooper pair wave function. This is accomplished by examining the deviation from ideal bosonic behavior through the correction to the Bose enhancement factor, a quantity intimately connected to the algebra of composite particle creation and annihilation operators. Unlike elementary bosons, composite pairs of fermions do not obey canonical bosonic commutation relations exactly; instead, the underlying fermionic substructure introduces corrections that become significant when the pair size becomes comparable to the interparticle spacing. By systematically calculating these corrections, one obtains a precise measure of how closely the pair wave function approximates that of an ideal boson, and how this approximation breaks down as the pairs become more weakly bound and spatially extended.

## Theoretical Framework: The Uniform Gas Model

To make the theoretical framework concrete and tractable, the analysis is illustrated using the example of a three-dimensional uniform Fermi gas. This idealized system, characterized by translational invariance and a well-defined Fermi wave vector $k_F$, allows for explicit analytical and numerical treatment of the pairing correlations across the crossover regime. The uniform gas serves as a foundational model that captures the essential physics of the BEC-BCS crossover without the additional complications introduced by trapping potentials, thereby providing clear insight into the fundamental relationship between interaction strength and pair statistics.

## Two Definitions of the Cooper Pair Wave Function

A key aspect of this work involves a careful comparison between two distinct, physically motivated definitions of the Cooper pair wave function:

1. **ODLRO-based definition**: This definition arises from the off-diagonal long-range order (ODLRO) exhibited by the two-particle density matrix in the superfluid phase. It captures the pairing correlations that are directly responsible for macroscopic quantum coherence and superfluidity, reflecting the long-distance behavior of the correlation function.

2. **Pair-projected BCS definition**: This alternative definition is constructed by projecting the standard BCS many-body wave function onto a fixed particle number sector, thereby extracting an explicit two-body pair wave function directly from the BCS ansatz.

While both definitions aim to characterize the same underlying physical phenomenon—the pairing of fermions into composite bosonic-like entities—they are constructed through different mathematical procedures and are not, in general, guaranteed to coincide across the entire crossover.

## Results: Crossover Behavior and Convergence

The comparison between these two definitions reveals a rich and nontrivial crossover behavior. On the **negative scattering length side** of the resonance (the BCS-like regime), the ODLRO-based Cooper pairs are found to exhibit a **more pronounced bosonic character** than the pair-projected counterparts. This suggests that the long-range coherence properties captured by ODLRO better reflect the emergent bosonic nature of the pairs than does the local pair-projection procedure in this weakly-interacting regime.

However, as the interaction strength is increased toward the **positive scattering length side**, the two definitions are found to **converge** in the regime where $(k_F a)^{-1} \gtrsim 1$. In this deep BEC regime, more than 90% of the atoms are found to occupy tightly bound molecular condensates. Here, the physical picture simplifies considerably: the pairs become so tightly bound and well-separated from one another that both definitions of the pair wave function accurately and consistently describe essentially ideal bosonic molecules, with the distinction between ODLRO-based and pair-projected definitions becoming immaterial.

## Significance

These findings provide important theoretical insight into the subtle differences between competing definitions of pairing correlations in strongly interacting Fermi gases, clarifying under what conditions such definitions can be used interchangeably and where genuine physical distinctions emerge. This has direct relevance for interpreting experimental measurements of pair correlations in ultracold atomic gases and for understanding the fundamental crossover from fermionic to bosonic quantum statistics in strongly correlated many-body systems.

# Bosonic Character of Cooper Pairs Across the BCS-BEC Crossover

## Introduction

The crossover from Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) superconductivity to Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) of tightly bound molecular pairs represents one of the most fertile testing grounds for many-body quantum theory. Ultracold Fermi gases with a Feshbach resonance provide an ideal experimental platform to explore this crossover, as the s-wave scattering length $a$ between fermionic atoms can be tuned continuously from large and negative (weakly attractive, BCS-like regime) through the unitary limit ($a \to \pm\infty$) to large and positive (strongly bound molecules, BEC-like regime). Throughout this crossover, pairs of fermions with opposite spin and momentum—Cooper pairs in the weak-coupling limit—evolve smoothly into tightly bound bosonic molecules in the strong-coupling limit. Understanding precisely how and when these fermionic pairs acquire genuinely bosonic statistical character is a fundamental question with implications for superfluidity, condensate fraction, and the applicability of effective bosonic theories across the crossover.

A central subtlety in this problem is that there is no unique, universally agreed-upon definition of the "Cooper pair wave function" in the many-body context. Different theoretical constructions—each physically motivated—can yield different predictions for how bosonic the pairs are as a function of interaction strength. In this study, we systematically compare two commonly employed definitions of the pair wave function and investigate the extent to which they capture equivalent physics as the system is tuned across the BCS-BEC crossover.

## Theoretical Framework

The first definition of the pair wave function is based on the off-diagonal long-range order (ODLRO) exhibited by the two-particle density matrix. In this approach, the pair wave function is identified with the leading eigenvector of the reduced two-body density matrix
$$
\rho_2(\mathbf{r}_1,\mathbf{r}_2;\mathbf{r}_1',\mathbf{r}_2') = \langle \Psi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}_1')\Psi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}_2')\Psi(\mathbf{r}_2)\Psi(\mathbf{r}_1)\rangle,
$$
in the limit of large particle separation. The macroscopic eigenvalue associated with this eigenvector quantifies the degree of pair condensation, in direct analogy to Penrose-Onsager criterion for single-particle Bose-Einstein condensation. This ODLRO-based pair wave function is a natural extension of the BEC order parameter to the case of composite bosons formed by two fermions, and it directly probes the coherence properties that underlie superfluidity.

The second definition arises from a real-space projection of the BCS wave function onto a fixed particle number. Starting from the standard BCS ansatz
$$
|\text{BCS}\rangle = \prod_{\mathbf{k}} \left(u_{\mathbf{k}} + v_{\mathbf{k}} c^\dagger_{\mathbf{k}\uparrow}c^\dagger_{-\mathbf{k}\downarrow}\right)|0\rangle,
$$
one can perform a particle-number projection to isolate the $N$-particle sector, yielding an explicit real-space pair wave function $\phi(\mathbf{r}) \propto \sum_{\mathbf{k}} (v_{\mathbf{k}}/u_{\mathbf{k}}) e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}$. This pair-projected wave function is the direct many-body generalization of the single Cooper pair wave function familiar from BCS theory, and it has the conceptual advantage of being explicitly derivable from the microscopic pairing amplitudes $u_{\mathbf{k}}, v_{\mathbf{k}}$ that emerge from the BCS mean-field gap and number equations.

While both definitions reduce to the same expression in certain limits, they are constructed from fundamentally different starting points: the ODLRO definition is an operationally defined many-body observable tied to long-range coherence, whereas the pair-projected definition is tied to the specific mean-field ansatz and its associated variational parameters. A key goal of this work is to quantify how these two definitions differ across the crossover and to what extent they yield consistent physical pictures of pair bosonization.

## Model and Methods

To perform this comparison in a controlled setting, we employ the three-dimensional uniform (homogeneous) Fermi gas model, in which finite-range trapping potentials are neglected and the system is treated as translationally invariant. This idealization removes confinement-induced inhomogeneities and allows the pairing physics to be analyzed purely as a function of the dimensionless interaction parameter $(k_F a)^{-1}$, where $k_F$ is the Fermi wave vector of the non-interacting gas. Working within the mean-field BCS framework extended self-consistently across the crossover (the "BCS-Leggett" approach), we solve the coupled gap and number equations at each value of $(k_F a)^{-1}$ to obtain the pairing amplitudes $u_{\mathbf{k}}$ and $v_{\mathbf{k}}$.

From these mean-field solutions, we construct both the ODLRO pair wave function, by diagonalizing the two-body density matrix in momentum space, and the pair-projected wave function, via direct evaluation of the projected BCS coefficients. To characterize the "bosonic character" of each pair wave function, we examine several complementary metrics: (i) the condensate fraction, defined as the largest eigenvalue of the (normalized) pair density matrix relative to the total pair number; (ii) the pair size, extracted from the spatial extent of $\phi(\mathbf{r})$ or the analogous ODLRO eigenvector in real space; and (iii) the degree to which the two-body wave function factorizes into a product of a smooth center-of-mass part and internal relative coordinate, a hallmark of an effective bosonic degree of freedom decoupled from the underlying fermionic substructure.

## Results

Our calculations reveal a clear and systematic distinction between the two pair wave function definitions on the BCS side of the crossover, i.e., for negative scattering length ($a<0$, $(k_F a)^{-1} < 0$). In this regime, the ODLRO-based pair wave function exhibits a markedly stronger bosonic character than the pair-projected wave function derived from the BCS ansatz. Specifically, the condensate fraction extracted from the ODLRO eigenvector remains sizable and the associated pair correlations decay more slowly, evincing coherence over larger length scales, than the corresponding quantities computed from the pair-projected definition. This discrepancy indicates that the long-range coherence captured by the two-body density matrix reflects collective, many-body correlations that are not fully captured by the single-pair projection of the mean-field state—the latter being more sensitive to the local, short-range pairing correlations that dominate the BCS regime, where Cooper pairs are large and strongly overlapping.

As the interaction strength is increased towards and through unitarity, and further into the BEC regime, the two definitions gradually converge. We find that for $(k_F a)^{-1} \gtrsim 1$, the ODLRO-based and pair-projected wave functions become essentially indistinguishable, both in their spatial profiles and in the extracted condensate fractions. In this strongly interacting, deeply bound regime, we find that over 90% of the atoms populate the molecular (bosonic) condensate, as measured by either definition of the pair wave function. This near-total condensation into tightly bound pairs signals the emergence of a genuinely bosonic gas of diatomic molecules, well described by a single, dominant two-body bound-state wave function—consistent with the expected BEC limit of the crossover, where pair binding energies far exceed the Fermi energy and pairs behave as pointlike composite bosons.

## Discussion and Conclusion

Taken together, these findings delineate a crossover in the degree of bosonic character exhibited by paired fermions, closely tracking—but not identical to—the more commonly discussed BCS-BEC crossover in the pairing gap and chemical potential. On the BCS side, the discrepancy between ODLRO- and pair-projection-based definitions underscores the fact that "Cooper pairs" in the weak-coupling regime are not well-described as simple, isolated two-body bound states; rather, their bosonic character is an emergent, collective property tied to the coherence of the many-body condensate as a whole, which the ODLRO measure captures more faithfully than a naive pairwise projection. This distinction has practical implications for effective bosonic descriptions (such as Gross-Pitaevskii-type theories) of the BCS regime, which may require care in specifying which underlying pair wave function is being used to define the effective bosonic field.

In contrast, the convergence of the two definitions in the regime $(k_F a)^{-1} \geq 1$ confirms that once pairs become sufficiently tightly bound, the specific choice of pair wave function definition becomes immaterial—the many-body coherence properties are then fully saturated by, and equivalent to, the two-body bound-state wave function of an isolated molecule. The finding that over 90% of atoms populate this molecular condensate provides a quantitative benchmark for the onset of a genuinely bosonic regime in the strongly interacting Fermi gas, complementing established diagnostics such as the pairing gap, molecular fraction from radiofrequency spectroscopy, and condensate fraction measurements from time-of-flight imaging in ultracold atom experiments.

More broadly, this work highlights the importance of carefully distinguishing between different, physically motivated definitions of pairing correlations when characterizing the crossover from fermionic to bosonic degrees of freedom. While mean-field BCS theory, extended across the crossover, provides a tractable framework for this comparison, our results suggest that future studies incorporating beyond-mean-field corrections—particularly on the BCS side, where quantum fluctuations and pairing fluctuations beyond the simple BCS ansatz are known to be significant—would be valuable to further refine the quantitative boundary between fermionic and bosonic pairing regimes. Such refinements would also help clarify the interpretation of experimental probes of pairing in strongly interacting Fermi gases realized with tunable Feshbach resonances.

# Feshbach Resonances in Ultracold Fermi Gases

The study of ultracold atomic gases has revolutionized our understanding of quantum many-body physics, and at the heart of this revolution lies a remarkable tool: the Feshbach resonance. This phenomenon allows experimentalists to precisely control the interaction strength between atoms using an external magnetic field, transforming simple atomic gases into versatile quantum simulators.

## The Physics of Fermi Gases

Fermi gases consist of particles obeying Fermi-Dirac statistics, meaning no two identical fermions can occupy the same quantum state due to the Pauli exclusion principle. When cooled to temperatures near absolute zero—often just billionths of a degree above 0 Kelvin—these gases exhibit striking quantum behavior. Unlike bosonic systems, which can condense into a single macroscopic quantum state (Bose-Einstein condensation), fermionic atoms must fill available energy states one by one, creating a characteristic "Fermi sea" of occupied states up to the Fermi energy.

The behavior of a Fermi gas depends critically on the interactions between particles. Without interactions, fermions simply stack into energy levels according to Pauli's principle. However, when interactions are introduced, entirely new phases of matter become accessible—including superfluidity, where fermions pair up and flow without resistance.

## The Role of Feshbach Resonances

This is where Feshbach resonances become indispensable. Named after physicist Herman Feshbach, who described the underlying scattering theory in nuclear physics context, these resonances occur when the energy of two colliding atoms in an open scattering channel matches the energy of a bound molecular state in a closed channel. By tuning an external magnetic field, physicists can bring these two channels into resonance, dramatically altering the effective interaction strength between atoms—from strongly repulsive to strongly attractive, passing through zero interaction at specific field values.

For fermionic atoms, this tunability opens the door to exploring the BEC-BCS crossover—a continuous transition between two seemingly distinct physical regimes:

- **BEC limit**: Strong attractive interactions cause fermions to form tightly bound molecular pairs, which then behave as bosons and can undergo Bose-Einstein condensation.
- **BCS limit**: Weak attractive interactions lead to the formation of loosely correlated Cooper pairs, analogous to the mechanism behind conventional superconductivity described by Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) theory.

## The Significance for Modern Physics

The ability to traverse this crossover in a controlled laboratory setting has profound implications. It provides insights into unconventional superconductivity, neutron star physics, and strongly correlated quantum systems that are otherwise difficult to study directly. The unitary regime—where the scattering length diverges near a Feshbach resonance—represents a particularly fascinating point where the gas exhibits universal behavior independent of the specific atomic species involved.

Experiments with fermionic isotopes such as lithium-6 and potassium-40 have exploited Feshbach resonances to create degenerate Fermi gases with tunable interactions, enabling precise measurements of thermodynamic quantities, collective excitations, and pairing gaps. These studies bridge atomic physics with condensed matter theory and nuclear physics, illustrating the deep interconnectedness of quantum phenomena across vastly different energy scales.

In conclusion, the marriage of Fermi statistics and Feshbach resonance physics has created one of the most powerful platforms in modern physics for exploring quantum many-body phenomena, offering a controllable, clean, and highly tunable system to probe fundamental questions about matter under extreme quantum conditions.

# Abstract

We investigate the bosonic character of Cooper pairs in a two-component Fermi gas near a Feshbach resonance, focusing on the crossover from weakly bound BCS-like pairs to tightly bound molecular bosons. Two distinct but frequently conflated definitions of the "pair wave function" are examined: (i) the two-particle reduced density matrix eigenfunction associated with off-diagonal long-range order (ODLRO), obtained from the anomalous average $\langle \psi_\uparrow^\dagger(\mathbf{r}_1)\psi_\downarrow^\dagger(\mathbf{r}_2)\rangle$, and (ii) the pair wave function extracted from a fixed-particle-number projection of the BCS variational state, $\phi(\mathbf{r}) \propto \int dk\, (v_k/u_k)\, e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}$. While both quantities reduce to the same expression in the extreme BEC limit, where they coincide with the two-body bound-state wave function of the Feshbach molecule, we show that they differ qualitatively in the BCS and crossover regimes. The ODLRO pair function retains long-range coherence and does not represent a normalizable two-body bound state except deep in the BEC regime, reflecting the many-body, extended nature of Cooper pairing. In contrast, the number-projected BCS pair wave function is normalizable at any coupling and exhibits a smooth evolution from a large, oscillatory Cooper-pair profile to a compact molecular bound state, providing a more faithful measure of pair "bosonization." We quantify the degree of bosonic behavior using the pair-condensate fraction, the two-body correlation length, and the deviation of the pair statistics from ideal Bose-Einstein behavior, computed self-consistently across the BEC-BCS crossover within mean-field and beyond-mean-field (Popov-corrected) treatments. Our results clarify the conditions under which Cooper pairs can be legitimately treated as structureless bosons, delineate the crossover scale at which pair-pair interactions and Pauli-blocking effects become significant, and reconcile the ODLRO and projected-BCS perspectives by relating them through the pair momentum distribution and closed-channel fraction. These findings have direct implications for interpreting condensate fraction measurements in ultracold Fermi gases and for constructing effective bosonic theories of the pseudogap and pairing regimes above $T_c$.

# Abstract

The crossover from Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) pairing to Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) in ultracold fermionic atom systems represents a paradigmatic testbed for many-body quantum physics, yet a quantitative measure of the bosonic character of composite pairs across this crossover remains an open challenge. In this work, we develop a framework for quantifying the BEC character of paired fermions by explicitly accounting for the Bose enhancement factor associated with the composite boson statistics of fermion pairs. Starting from the pair wavefunction and the many-body ground state constructed via a generalized BCS ansatz, we derive a correction to the condensate fraction that incorporates bosonic stimulation effects arising from the internal structure and finite size of the fermion pairs, going beyond the standard mean-field treatment that treats pairs as ideal point-like bosons. This correction becomes significant as the pair size becomes comparable to the interparticle spacing, precisely in the regime where deviations from ideal BEC behavior are expected to be most pronounced.

We apply this formalism to the paradigmatic case of a three-dimensional uniform Fermi gas with tunable s-wave interactions, computing the corrected condensate fraction as a function of the dimensionless interaction parameter $1/(k_F a)$ across the full BCS-BEC crossover. Our results show that the Bose-enhanced condensate fraction deviates appreciably from the conventional pair condensate fraction obtained from the Cooper pair wavefunction overlap, particularly in the crossover region, while recovering the expected ideal Bose gas limit deep in the BEC regime and vanishing appropriately in the weak-coupling BCS limit. We further examine the dependence of this correction on density and temperature, demonstrating that the Bose enhancement contribution provides a more faithful diagnostic of the emergent bosonic character of the paired fermions than pair correlation measures alone. These findings offer a refined and physically transparent metric for characterizing the BEC limit in strongly interacting Fermi gases, with direct relevance to ongoing experiments in ultracold atomic gases and potential extensions to nuclear and condensed matter pairing phenomena.

# Abstract

The characterization of Cooper pair bosonic character across the BEC-BCS crossover remains sensitive to the theoretical definition employed for the pair wavefunction, yet systematic comparisons between competing formalisms remain scarce. We investigate how two principal definitions—the off-diagonal long-range order (ODLRO) eigenfunction of the two-body density matrix and the pair-projected wavefunction obtained via number-projection onto the BCS ground state—yield quantitatively and qualitatively distinct assessments of pair bosonization throughout the crossover. Using a mean-field BCS framework supplemented by pair-correlation diagnostics, we compute the pair size, condensate fraction, and deviation from ideal Bose-Einstein statistics as functions of the interaction parameter $(k_F a)^{-1}$. We find that while both definitions coincide qualitatively in the extreme BEC limit, where pairs approach tightly bound, non-overlapping bosonic dimers, they diverge markedly in the crossover and unitary regimes. The ODLRO-based measure, tied to the natural orbital occupation of the two-particle density matrix, saturates more gradually and remains sensitive to residual fermionic exchange correlations even at moderately large $(k_F a)^{-1}$. In contrast, the pair-projected wavefunction, which explicitly enforces fixed particle number, exhibits a sharper onset of bosonic saturation and predicts a higher effective condensate fraction near $(k_F a)^{-1} \gtrsim 1$. This discrepancy arises from the differing treatment of number fluctuations and off-diagonal coherence inherent to each formalism: ODLRO measures genuine long-range coherence in the grand-canonical ensemble, whereas pair-projection captures short-range pairing correlations reorganized into a canonical-ensemble bosonic amplitude. Our results indicate that conclusions regarding the "degree of bosonization" of Cooper pairs are not solely a physical statement about the many-body state but are intrinsically entangled with the chosen operational definition. We discuss implications for interpreting condensate fraction measurements in ultracold Fermi gases and for benchmarking effective bosonic theories of the crossover, emphasizing that definition-dependent artifacts must be disentangled from genuine physical crossover behavior when quantifying pairing bosonicity near unitarity.

# Two-Particle Wave Function of Paired Atoms in a Tunable Fermi Gas: Bosonic Character Across the BEC-BCS Crossover

## Abstract

We investigate the two-particle wave function of paired fermionic atoms in a tunable Fermi gas across the BEC-BCS crossover, with particular emphasis on quantifying the bosonic character of these pairs as the interaction strength is varied via a Feshbach resonance. Starting from the mean-field BCS-Leggett ground state, we construct the two-particle reduced density matrix and extract the associated pair wave function, examining its spatial extent, internal structure, and momentum distribution as functions of the dimensionless interaction parameter $1/(k_F a)$. To characterize the degree to which these fermion pairs behave as effective composite bosons, we employ and compare two complementary theoretical definitions of "bosonic character": (i) a definition based on the deviation of the pair-pair correlation function from that of ideal, non-interacting bosons, which quantifies residual Pauli-exclusion effects among constituent fermions, and (ii) a definition rooted in the condensate depletion and the ratio of the anomalous pair amplitude to the total pair density, which measures how closely the many-body pair statistics approach true bosonic saturation. We show that on the BEC side ($1/(k_F a) \gg 0$), where pairs form tightly bound dimers with size much smaller than the interparticle spacing, both definitions converge and indicate near-ideal bosonic behavior, consistent with the expected mapping onto a weakly interacting Bose gas of molecules. In contrast, on the BCS side ($1/(k_F a) \ll 0$), where the pair size (of order the coherence length $\xi$) greatly exceeds the interparticle spacing, the two definitions diverge substantially: the correlation-function-based measure reveals strong deviations from bosonic statistics due to Pauli blocking among overlapping Cooper pairs, while the condensate-depletion-based measure can remain misleadingly close to unity due to the macroscopic occupation of the pair correlation itself. We discuss the origin of this discrepancy in terms of the internal fermionic substructure that becomes probed at length scales below the pair size, and we relate our findings to the crossover in the pair-breaking excitation spectrum and the evolution of the contact parameter. Our results clarify the regime of validity of the "composite boson" picture often invoked to describe the BEC-BCS crossover, and highlight the necessity of carefully specifying the operational definition of pair bosonic character when interpreting experiments—such as those probing molecular condensate fractions or pair correlations via noise correlation and RF spectroscopy—performed at finite $1/(k_F a)$ in ultracold Fermi gases.

# Molecular Condensate Fraction and Bosonic Enhancement in a Feshbach-Tuned Fermi Gas: Contrasting ODLRO and Pair-Projected Approaches

**Abstract**

We present a theoretical analysis of the molecular condensate fraction in an ultracold Fermi gas across the BCS-BEC crossover, tuned via a Feshbach resonance, with particular attention to the role of bosonic enhancement factors in the condensate depletion. Two complementary formalisms for characterizing off-diagonal long-range order (ODLRO) in the two-body density matrix are compared: the standard many-body approach based on the largest eigenvalue of the reduced pair density matrix, and a pair-projected wave function method derived from a fixed particle-number BCS-like ansatz. While both approaches converge to identical results in the extreme BEC limit, where the system reduces to a dilute gas of tightly bound bosonic dimers, they exhibit systematic discrepancies of order $1/N$ and beyond in the crossover and BCS regimes, stemming from differing treatments of pair correlations and number-fluctuation effects inherent to the grand-canonical mean-field description.

We derive closed-form expressions for the condensate fraction $N_0/N_{pairs}$ within each framework and show that the pair-projected approach naturally incorporates bosonic enhancement factors of the form $(1+n_k)$ associated with stimulated pairing into already-occupied momentum modes, analogous to the enhancement seen in the Bogoliubov theory of interacting bosons. In contrast, the ODLRO eigenvalue approach, formulated through the two-particle correlation function $\langle \psi^\dagger(\mathbf{r})\psi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}')\psi(\mathbf{r}'')\psi(\mathbf{r}''')\rangle$, captures the same physics through the anomalous averages of the BCS wave function but does not manifestly separate the enhancement contribution from the underlying fermionic pair susceptibility. We quantify the difference between the two condensate fractions as a function of the scattering length $a$ and interaction parameter $1/(k_F a)$, identifying the unitary regime as the point of maximal sensitivity to the choice of formalism.

Our results clarify the correspondence between fermionic pairing theories and bosonic condensate observables measurable via rf spectroscopy and molecular photoassociation experiments, and provide a framework for interpreting condensate fraction measurements in $^{40}$K and $^6$Li Feshbach-resonant gases. We further discuss implications for the applicability of Penrose-Onsager criteria to fermionic pair condensates and the extent to which molecular BEC statistics are recovered in the strongly bound-pair limit, offering guidance for future experiments probing the interplay between pairing correlations and bosonic coherence across the crossover.
